title: Genetic Skin Conditions: Albinism and Ehlers-Danlos Syndrome
subject: Integumentary System (INTG)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter takes two inherited skin disorders down to the molecule. In albinism the melanocytes are present in normal numbers but cannot finish making melanin, so the skin, hair, and eyes lack their pigment shield and the developing visual pathway never forms correctly. In Ehlers-Danlos syndrome the collagen fibril is built or processed incorrectly, so skin, joints, vessels, and hollow organs lose tensile strength. Board questions usually give a child or young adult with a physical finding and ask for the missing enzyme, the collagen type, the mode of inheritance, or the complication that follows. The reasoning runs from the defective protein to the tissue that depends on it.

Enzyme cofactor chemistry: copper, iron, vitamin C, and alpha-ketoglutarate dependent hydroxylation

connections.how: Albinism is a failure of melanin synthesis with melanocytes present, while vitiligo is loss of the melanocytes themselves, so the two sit at opposite ends of the same pigment pathway.
Vitamin C and copper deficiency strike the same hydroxylation and cross-linking steps that are mutated in kyphoscoliotic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, so scurvy and Menkes disease mimic parts of it.

connections.to: Malignant skin neoplasms (IN-13-G) and skin genetics (IN-7)
connections.how: Melanin absorbs ultraviolet photons and limits pyrimidine dimer formation, so the unpigmented epidermis of albinism accumulates the mutations that drive squamous and basal cell carcinoma early.

connections.to: Immune responses and infection in skin disease (IN-9, IN-11)
connections.how: Chediak-Higashi syndrome couples partial albinism to failed lysosomal delivery in neutrophils and cytotoxic lymphocytes, which explains its recurrent pyogenic infections.
Marfan syndrome and osteogenesis imperfecta share joint laxity with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome but differ in the defective protein, so they are separated by the organs that fail.
Scar strength depends on type I fibril assembly and cross-linking, which is why Ehlers-Danlos wounds heal slowly and widen into thin atrophic scars.

sections.title: Oculocutaneous albinism: a synthetic block with melanocytes intact

blocks.text: Melanocytes are neural crest derived cells that settle in the basal layer of the epidermis and in the hair bulb, where roughly one melanocyte serves about ten basal keratinocytes. Inside each melanocyte, melanin is built within melanosomes, lysosome-related organelles that import tyrosine and the enzymes that act on it. Tyrosinase, a copper-containing enzyme, hydroxylates tyrosine to DOPA and then oxidizes DOPA to dopaquinone; everything downstream of dopaquinone proceeds largely without enzymatic help toward eumelanin or pheomelanin. Mature melanosomes travel out along melanocyte dendrites and are handed to surrounding keratinocytes, where the pigment forms a supranuclear cap that intercepts ultraviolet photons before they reach DNA.

blocks.title: Melanin synthesis and transfer
steps: Tyrosine is taken into the melanosome of the melanocyte
Dopaquinone polymerizes to eumelanin or pheomelanin
Mature melanosomes move along dendrites to keratinocytes
Melanin caps keratinocyte nuclei and absorbs ultraviolet light
blocks.caption: Albinism interrupts this chain at the enzyme or at melanosome function; the melanocytes themselves remain in place.

blocks.text: Oculocutaneous albinism is a group of autosomal recessive disorders of this pathway. The key teaching point is that melanocyte number and distribution are normal, and so is their position in the basal layer on biopsy; what fails is pigment production. In the classic form, OCA1, both copies of the tyrosinase gene are defective, so the committed step cannot run. A complete loss of activity gives white hair, milk-white skin, and blue-gray translucent irides that never darken, while partial activity allows some pigment to accumulate with age and, in temperature sensitive variants, allows pigment to appear in cooler regions such as the limbs while warmer central areas stay pale. Other forms lose melanosomal membrane proteins rather than the enzyme: OCA2 affects the P protein and is the form most often seen in populations of African ancestry, OCA3 affects tyrosinase-related protein 1 and often produces reddish-brown pigment, and OCA4 affects a melanosomal transporter.

blocks.caption: All forms are autosomal recessive, and in all of them melanocyte numbers are normal.

blocks.text: Two sets of consequences follow. In the skin, melanin is the main physical filter for ultraviolet light and also quenches the radicals that ultraviolet exposure generates, so without it keratinocytes accumulate cyclobutane pyrimidine dimers and other photoproducts with every exposure. Sunburn occurs at trivial doses, solar elastosis and actinic keratoses appear in childhood or early adult life, and squamous cell and basal cell carcinoma arise decades earlier than expected; melanoma also occurs and is often amelanotic, which makes it harder to recognize. In the eye, melanin within the retinal pigment epithelium is required for normal central retinal development and for the correct routing of retinal ganglion cell axons at the optic chiasm. Its absence produces foveal hypoplasia with acuity commonly in the 20/100 to 20/400 range, infantile nystagmus, photophobia, iris transillumination, strabismus, and poor stereopsis from axonal misrouting.

blocks.predict: A newborn has white hair and skin. Would you expect abnormal catecholamine levels, since both melanin and catecholamines start from tyrosine?
blocks.explain: No. Catecholamine synthesis begins with tyrosine hydroxylase in neurons and chromaffin cells, a different enzyme in a different compartment. Tyrosinase works only inside melanosomes, so its loss removes pigment without touching dopamine, norepinephrine, or epinephrine.
blocks.check: Compare the first paragraph of this section with the catecholamine pathway you learned in endocrine biochemistry.

sections.title: Separating oculocutaneous albinism from ocular albinism and the trafficking disorders

blocks.text: Hypopigmentation has several mechanisms, and the exam separates them by asking which tissues are involved, how the trait is inherited, and whether melanocytes are present. Ocular albinism is X-linked and results from loss of GPR143, a melanosomal membrane protein needed chiefly in the eye and in the retinal pigment epithelium. Affected boys have the full ocular picture of nystagmus, low acuity, foveal hypoplasia, and iris transillumination with skin and hair pigment that falls within or close to the family range. Because X inactivation is mosaic, carrier mothers are usually asymptomatic but show patchy fundus pigmentation on examination, a finding that confirms the inheritance pattern when a pedigree is ambiguous.

Chediak-Higashi syndrome is autosomal recessive and caused by defects in LYST, a regulator of the fission and fusion of lysosomes and other lysosome-related organelles. The pigment defect is partial rather than complete: melanosomes clump into giant macromelanosomes that are poorly transferred, giving silvery hair, pale skin, and ocular findings milder than in oculocutaneous albinism. The same trafficking failure produces the rest of the syndrome. Neutrophils and monocytes contain giant granules on a peripheral smear but cannot deliver them into the phagosome, so patients have recurrent pyogenic skin and respiratory infections, typically with Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci. Natural killer cells and cytotoxic T lymphocytes cannot release their lytic granules, which allows an accelerated phase resembling hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis. Platelet dense granules are deficient, so bleeding time is prolonged with a normal platelet count, and progressive peripheral neuropathy develops as abnormal organelles accumulate in long axons.

blocks.title: Disorders of reduced skin and ocular pigment
rows: Generalized pale skin and hair plus nystagmus and low acuity
Ocular findings in boys, near normal skin, patchy fundus in carriers
Silvery hair, giant neutrophil granules, pyogenic infections, neuropathy, bleeding
Albinism with platelet storage pool bleeding, pulmonary fibrosis, granulomatous colitis
Sharply marginated depigmented macules on previously normal skin
Stable white forelock and ventral patches present from birth
Diffuse light pigment with intellectual disability and a musty odor
blocks.caption: Melanocytes present but unproductive points to a synthetic or trafficking defect; melanocytes absent points to destruction or failed migration.

blocks.text: Two entries on that table reward a second look. Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome belongs with Chediak-Higashi as a disorder of lysosome-related organelle biogenesis, and it is recognized by albinism plus a platelet storage pool defect with mucosal bleeding, with pulmonary fibrosis and granulomatous colitis developing in some subtypes. Phenylketonuria dilutes pigment for a biochemical reason worth naming: phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency blocks the conversion of phenylalanine to tyrosine, so tyrosine becomes a dietary requirement, and the accumulated phenylalanine also inhibits tyrosinase directly. The result is light hair and skin in a child whose dominant problem is neurological rather than cutaneous.

blocks.predict: A boy has nystagmus and a translucent iris but hair and skin that match his siblings. His mother's fundus shows patchy pigment. Which diagnosis fits, and why is the skin spared?
blocks.explain: X-linked ocular albinism. GPR143 is required mainly for melanosome maturation in the eye and retinal pigment epithelium, so cutaneous melanocytes pigment adequately. The mother's mottled fundus reflects random X inactivation in a carrier.

sections.title: Collagen synthesis and the molecular basis of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

blocks.text: Fibrillar collagen is a rope of three polypeptide chains wound into a right-handed triple helix. Each chain repeats the sequence glycine, X, Y, with proline or hydroxyproline common at X and Y, because glycine is the only residue small enough to pack along the crowded helical axis. Inside the cell, prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases add hydroxyl groups using molecular oxygen, alpha-ketoglutarate, ferrous iron, and vitamin C as the reducing agent that keeps the iron active. Hydroxyproline stabilizes the helix by hydrogen bonding, and hydroxylysine provides sites for sugars and for later covalent cross-links. Because assembly runs through many steps, a defect at any one of them produces a recognizable disease.

blocks.title: Collagen assembly from gene to fiber
steps: Pro-alpha chains with Gly-X-Y repeats are translated into the rough endoplasmic reticulum
Prolyl and lysyl hydroxylases hydroxylate residues, requiring vitamin C
Three chains wind into a procollagen triple helix and are secreted
N and C procollagen peptidases cleave the propeptides to give tropocollagen
Copper-dependent lysyl oxidase cross-links fibrils into mature fibers
blocks.caption: Ehlers-Danlos subtypes, scurvy, Menkes disease, and osteogenesis imperfecta each interrupt a different step of this one pathway.

blocks.text: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is not one disease but a family of defects in collagen structure or processing, and the protein involved predicts which tissues fail. The classic type is autosomal dominant and usually follows mutations in COL5A1 or COL5A2, which encode type V collagen. Type V is quantitatively minor, but it nucleates type I fibrils and limits their diameter, so when it is reduced or abnormal the dermis fills with irregular, oversized, poorly organized fibrils. The skin stretches and the joints are lax while elastin remains normal, which is why the skin recoils rather than hanging loosely. The vascular type, also autosomal dominant, arises from mutations in COL3A1. Type III collagen is a major fibrillar collagen of the media and adventitia of arteries, of bowel wall, of uterus, and of early granulation tissue, so these are the structures that tear. The kyphoscoliotic type is autosomal recessive and reflects deficiency of lysyl hydroxylase 1, encoded by PLOD1; underhydroxylated lysine cannot form stable cross-links, so collagen in sclera, ligament, and paraspinal tissue stays weak.

blocks.title: Where the pathway breaks and what results
rows: Bone fragility, blue sclerae, hearing loss
Hyperextensible fragile skin, lax joints, atrophic scars
Perifollicular hemorrhage, bleeding gums, poor wound healing
blocks.caption: Nutritional and genetic lesions converge on the same steps, which is why scurvy and Menkes disease resemble parts of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome.

blocks.title: Worked example: reading the subtype from one laboratory clue
blocks.text: A boy has severe hypotonia at birth, progressive scoliosis, hyperextensible skin, and a scleral rupture after minor trauma. Urine collagen cross-link analysis shows a high ratio of lysyl pyridinoline to hydroxylysyl pyridinoline. Work backward: the cross-links present are the ones made from lysine that was never hydroxylated, so the missing activity is lysyl hydroxylase 1, the product of PLOD1. That places the case in the kyphoscoliotic type, explains why both parents are unaffected carriers in an autosomal recessive trait, and predicts fragile sclera and ligament rather than the arterial rupture of the type III defect.

Two further subtypes are worth keeping straight. The hypermobile type is the most common clinically and is diagnosed on joint hypermobility, soft skin, and chronic pain without a consistently identified gene, so a question that gives hypermobility with no molecular clue usually points here. The arthrochalasia type removes the N-propeptide cleavage site of type I collagen and presents with congenital bilateral hip dislocation and extreme laxity, a reminder that the same gene gives a joint phenotype or a fracture phenotype depending on the domain affected.

sections.title: Skin, joint, and vascular findings of Ehlers-Danlos syndrome

blocks.text: The cutaneous examination follows directly from disorganized dermal fibrils. Skin feels velvety and doughy and can be lifted several centimeters away from the forearm or neck, then snaps back cleanly because elastin is intact; this is hyperextensibility rather than the loose redundant skin of an elastin disorder. The dermis tears under shear that normal skin tolerates, so minor trauma produces gaping wounds, sutures pull through, and bruising appears after contact the patient cannot recall. Healing is slow and mechanically poor, because scar tensile strength depends on new type I fibrils being assembled and cross-linked, so scars widen under resting skin tension into thin, wrinkled, atrophic cigarette-paper plaques. Over repeatedly injured pressure points such as knees, elbows, and shins, piled scar tissue and fat form soft molluscoid pseudotumors, and mobile calcified subcutaneous spheroids may be felt along the shins and forearms.

Joints are hypermobile because ligament and capsule collagen is weak, and hypermobility is quantified with the nine point Beighton score. Recurrent subluxation and dislocation of shoulders, patellae, and digits, chronic joint and muscle pain, flat feet, early osteoarthritis from repeated microtrauma, and gingival and periodontal fragility are all common. Mitral valve prolapse appears more often than in the general population because valve leaflets also depend on fibrillar collagen.

The vascular type deserves separate attention because its complications are lethal and its skin is different in character. Rather than markedly hyperextensible skin, these patients have thin translucent skin over the chest and abdomen with an unusually visible venous pattern, aged-looking hands with prominent tendons, called acrogeria, and a characteristic face with thin lips, a pinched nose, hollow cheeks, and prominent eyes. The mechanical problem is that type III collagen bears much of the circumferential load in the media and adventitia of medium caliber arteries and in the walls of bowel and uterus. Wall tension rises with the product of transmural pressure and radius divided by wall thickness, so a wall that cannot carry that tension dissects or ruptures without antecedent aneurysm, often in the second to fourth decade. Spontaneous rupture or dissection of mesenteric, splenic, renal, or iliac arteries, perforation of the sigmoid colon in the absence of diverticulitis, uterine rupture in late pregnancy or at delivery, carotid-cavernous fistula, and intracranial berry aneurysms are the characteristic events.

blocks.predict: Two young adults both have hypermobile fingers and easy bruising. One has velvety skin that lifts far from the forearm with wide scars on both knees; the other has thin skin with visible chest veins and no unusual scars. Which one needs vascular imaging?
blocks.explain: The second. Thin translucent skin with a visible venous pattern and relatively unremarkable scarring points to a COL3A1 defect, where the clinical danger is arterial, bowel, and uterine rupture. The first picture, dominated by stretchy skin and wide atrophic scars, fits the classic type, whose risks are cutaneous and articular.

sections.title: Distinguishing Ehlers-Danlos syndrome from Marfan syndrome and osteogenesis imperfecta

blocks.text: All three disorders can present with lax joints and a family history, so they are separated by the defective protein and by the organ that fails first. Marfan syndrome is autosomal dominant and follows mutations in FBN1, which encodes fibrillin-1, the scaffold protein of elastic microfibrils. Fibrillin also binds latent transforming growth factor beta and keeps it sequestered, so when fibrillin is abnormal excess signaling by that growth factor degrades the aortic media, and the aorta dilates at the root and may dissect. The skeleton is tall and slender with arm span exceeding height, a reduced upper to lower segment ratio, arachnodactyly, pectus deformity, scoliosis, and joint laxity. The lens subluxates upward because the zonular fibers are rich in fibrillin, and mitral valve prolapse, dural ectasia, and spontaneous pneumothorax complete the picture. The skin shows striae but is neither hyperextensible nor fragile.

Osteogenesis imperfecta is most often autosomal dominant and arises from mutations in COL1A1 or COL1A2. A mutation that produces an abnormal chain acts in a dominant negative way, spoiling every helix that contains it, which is why structural mutations are generally more severe than those that merely halve the amount of normal collagen. Because type I collagen dominates bone matrix, dentin, sclera, and the ossicular chain, the phenotype is recurrent fractures with minimal trauma, bowing and short stature, blue or gray sclerae from a thin sclera that lets choroidal pigment show through, conductive or mixed hearing loss, and opalescent fragile teeth. Joint laxity occurs, but fractures dominate the history.

blocks.caption: Homocystinuria is included because its marfanoid habitus is a standard distractor; the direction of lens displacement and the inheritance pattern separate it.

blocks.title: Worked example: one finding at a time
blocks.text: A 19 year old is 193 cm tall with long fingers, lax joints, and a dislocated lens. First ask the direction of lens displacement. Upward points to fibrillin-1 and Marfan syndrome, so the aortic root is the organ at risk. Downward points to homocystinuria, an autosomal recessive enzyme defect with thromboembolic rather than aneurysmal risk, confirmed biochemically by elevated plasma homocysteine. If instead the lens is normal but the skin lifts far off the forearm and old scars are wide and papery, the answer moves to classic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome. If the history is of several fractures in childhood with gray-blue sclerae, it moves to osteogenesis imperfecta.

A practical sequence helps with a mixed picture. Ask first whether bones fracture, which isolates osteogenesis imperfecta. Ask next whether the aorta dilates and the lens is displaced, which isolates Marfan syndrome and its mimics. Ask then whether the skin itself is abnormal, stretchy and fragile with atrophic scars or thin and translucent, which isolates Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and names the subtype. Two caveats keep the reasoning honest: aortic root dilation also occurs in some Ehlers-Danlos and related conditions, so it is suggestive rather than diagnostic, and joint hypermobility alone is far too common to decide anything.

integration.text: These two disorders show how one molecular lesion reaches several disciplines at once. In albinism, embryology supplies neural crest derived melanocytes that migrate normally, histology confirms them present in the basal layer, biochemistry names the copper-dependent tyrosinase step that fails, neuroscience explains why absent retinal pigment epithelium melanin leaves a hypoplastic fovea and misrouted chiasmal axons, and pathology supplies the ultraviolet mutagenesis that brings keratinocyte carcinoma forward by decades. The trafficking disorders add immunology: when LYST fails, the same organelle defect that clumps melanosomes also keeps neutrophil granules out of phagosomes and lytic granules inside cytotoxic lymphocytes, so partial albinism travels with pyogenic infection and an uncontrolled inflammatory phase.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome makes the same point along the collagen pathway. Biochemistry gives the steps, nutrition gives the cofactors so that vitamin C and copper deficiency reproduce parts of the phenotype, anatomy explains why type III collagen loss endangers arteries, sigmoid colon, and uterus, and pathology of wound healing explains the widened atrophic scar. The limits are worth stating plainly. Subtype classification has been revised repeatedly and more than a dozen types are now recognized, genotype does not fully predict severity, the hypermobile type has no reliable molecular marker, and a mutation in the same gene can give different diseases depending on the domain affected, as type I collagen mutations produce either fractures or congenital hip dislocation. For board purposes, learn the four or five subtypes with a named protein and reason from the protein to the tissue.

summary: In oculocutaneous albinism, melanocyte number is normal and pigment production fails; in vitiligo and piebaldism the melanocytes are absent from affected skin.
Tyrosinase, a copper-containing melanosomal enzyme, converts tyrosine to DOPA and DOPA to dopaquinone; catecholamine synthesis uses tyrosine hydroxylase instead and is unaffected.
Without melanin, ultraviolet light reaches keratinocyte DNA, so sunburn, actinic damage, and squamous and basal cell carcinoma appear decades early.
Retinal pigment epithelium melanin guides foveal development and chiasmal axon routing, which is why albinism causes foveal hypoplasia, nystagmus, low acuity, and poor stereopsis.

Ocular albinism is X-linked with near normal skin; Chediak-Higashi syndrome is an autosomal recessive LYST trafficking defect with partial albinism, giant granules, pyogenic infections, bleeding, and neuropathy.

Collagen requires glycine every third residue, vitamin C dependent hydroxylation, propeptide cleavage, and copper-dependent lysyl oxidase cross-linking; a lesion at each step names a different disease.
Classic Ehlers-Danlos syndrome reflects type V collagen (COL5A1), which controls type I fibril diameter, and gives hyperextensible fragile skin, hypermobility, and wide atrophic scars.

Vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome reflects type III collagen (COL3A1) and predicts arterial dissection or rupture, sigmoid perforation, uterine rupture, and berry aneurysms, often without prior aneurysm.
The kyphoscoliotic type is autosomal recessive lysyl hydroxylase 1 deficiency, with congenital hypotonia, progressive scoliosis, and fragile sclerae.
Marfan syndrome is fibrillin-1 with aortic root dilation and upward lens subluxation; osteogenesis imperfecta is type I collagen with fractures, blue sclerae, and hearing loss.

verify: Subtype names and counts for Ehlers-Danlos syndrome follow the current international classification, which has been revised more than once; confirm which subtype names and how many types NABNE expects.
The relative frequency of oculocutaneous albinism subtypes varies by population and by source, and prevalence figures were therefore not stated; confirm whether NABNE expects any prevalence numbers.
Visual acuity in albinism is commonly quoted as 20/100 to 20/400, but texts give slightly different ranges; treat the range as approximate.
The melanocyte to basal keratinocyte ratio is given as about one to ten here, with sources ranging from roughly one in four to one in ten depending on body site; confirm the figure expected.

Whether NABNE tests Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome, Griscelli syndrome, piebaldism, dermatosparaxis, or arthrochalasia by name, or only albinism and the main Ehlers-Danlos types, needs checking against current official materials.

Urine lysyl pyridinoline to hydroxylysyl pyridinoline testing for the kyphoscoliotic type is used in reference laboratories; confirm whether a laboratory confirmation method is within Part I scope before relying on the worked example clue.

Requested new diagram names for a future revision: melanin-pathway (tyrosine to dopaquinone to eumelanin and pheomelanin inside the melanosome, with transfer to keratinocytes) and collagen-assembly (intracellular hydroxylation and helix formation, secretion, propeptide cleavage, fibril assembly, and lysyl oxidase cross-linking, with the disease that matches each step).
